mappings.note: First half names the stored form (elastic PE), which is LO-5; second half asks how more stretch sends the projectile further, which is the PE-to-KE conversion, LO-7. The paired L62 item stops at the naming and so carries LO-5 alone.

Part (a) labels effort and load on a lever - identification of the machine and its parts (LO-3); part (b) is the moment/mechanical-advantage balance, which only C2.6 names. Weight difference is explained by arm lengths, not by any energy outcome.

The answer is that energy is what lets the ball exert a force and move the wickets - energy as the capacity to do work, which is LO-4's 'explain the concept of energy'. Not LO-5: no form is named and no conversion is traced.
Defines kinetic energy as the motion component of mechanical energy - the define-KE clause of LO-5. Definitional only, so neither LO-6 nor LO-7 applies.
Pure recall of 1/2 mv^2, which LO-5 covers as deriving/stating the expression. LO-6 is reserved for items that substitute values, such as the doubling-velocity item next to it.

Applies the squared-velocity dependence to get a factor of four - using the expression, LO-6. One of three near-identical doubling items in the chapter that honestly share this outcome; format is the only difference.

Two properties asked: KE is a scalar (a fact about the quantity, LO-5) and it rises when positive work is done, which is the work-energy theorem (LO-3). The second clause is what separates this from the other scalar-KE item, which stops at the formula.
Deformation stores elastic potential energy - naming a form of energy, LO-5. No release or conversion is asked about, so LO-7 stays out, unlike the projectile version of the same rubber band.

Greater height means greater PE, which becomes greater KE on falling and so a deeper crater - a PE-to-KE argument under free fall, LO-7. Not LO-6: the answer is comparative, with no energy value computed.
Recall of mgh, the derive-PE clause of LO-5. Identical demand to MCQ O23; the frame gives no way to separate a recall in MCQ form from one in written form.

Work done against attraction is stored as potential energy in a magnetic configuration - potential energy by configuration, which is LO-5's PE clause generalised beyond height. Not LO-2: the work is invoked qualitatively, never computed.

Defines mechanical energy as the sum of KE and PE - naming a form of energy in terms of its two components, LO-5. LO-4 would fit a question about energy in general; this one is specifically about the mechanical form.

The verb is STATE THE LAW, which is C-2.6-LO-1's own wording, applied to LO-7's free-fall case. Sibling item L68 asks instead what happens mechanically, so it takes LO-7 alone - the statement/mechanism split is the discriminator.

Asks the CONSEQUENCE of falling PE during free fall - an exactly equal rise in KE. That is the mechanism clause of LO-7, not the law statement, which is why C-2.6-LO-1 is withheld here but used on L67.

Definition of work plus the full positive/negative/zero sign taxonomy with examples. All of it comes from the definition of work and the force-displacement direction, so LO-1 alone; W = F x s appears as a statement, not a calculation.

Part (b) is the PE/KE swap across the swing (LO-7), part (c) needs energy conserved but lost to friction (C-2.6-LO-1), and part (a) requires producing the labelled extreme/mean-position representation (C8.1). Three parts, three codes.

Parts (a) and (b) are chains and distinctions between forms of energy (LO-5); part (c) asks why machines stop when the supply is cut, which is the conservation law with dissipation (C-2.6-LO-1). LO-7 is not cited: the dam's fall is one link in a longer chain, not the subject.

The scientific conception of work, its two conditions, and contrasting examples - all definitional, LO-1. This is the long-answer twin of V49/S79; the added examples do not change which outcome is tested.
Defines KE and PE and derives 1/2 mv^2 (both LO-5 clauses), then asks for the work/change-in-KE relation, which is the work-energy theorem (LO-3). Same pairing as S85, with the PE definition added.

The stem names the law of conservation of ENERGY (not just mechanical) and asks why the real pendulum stops - squarely C-2.6-LO-1, with LO-7 for the PE/KE interchange used to illustrate it. Ordering reflects that the law, not the swing, is the subject.
Defines power and the watt (C-2.6-LO-1) and computes 1200 J over 120 s (C-2.6-LO-2). The 'average power' part is a gloss on the same definition, so it needs no third code.

Describes the forms of energy and gives interconversion examples - the two clauses of LO-5 together. Deliberately not C-2.6-LO-1: the item asks whether forms convert, not whether the total is conserved.

The KE that vanishes at impact must go somewhere, so the answer is the conservation law (C-2.6-LO-1); LO-7 supplies the preceding free-fall build-up of that KE. Contrast L68, where the object never lands and the law is never invoked.

POOR FIT. Only the pulley identification (LO-3) and the diagram construction (C8.1) are genuinely covered; the graded physics is velocity ratio and efficiency, neither of which exists anywhere in curriculum 82, and MA is reachable only through the competency C2.6.
One substitution into W = F x s giving 20 J - the purest instance of LO-2 in the chapter, and the reason LO-2 is held back from the many definition-only work items.
